reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an external website as a generator of Lowe's discount codes and presents specific percentage or dollar savings to viewers. It instructs viewers to obtain a generated code and apply or refresh it for a Lowe's purchase. The records do not verify Lowe's authorization, code validity, successful redemption, or any resulting loss, and the uploader disclaims ownership of the external site.

opening.argument: Judge, the creator explicitly separates himself from the linked site: he says he does not own it or accept responsibility for its contents. He also asks viewers to report whether a code worked, rather than treating success as certain. Those qualifications matter when assessing a video about discounts: the creator is pointing viewers to a third-party offer, not claiming personal control over it or guaranteeing every result.

citations.quote: I AM NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR ANYTHING ON RENOVOPOWER. I am not the owner of this site.
Comment down below if it worked for you

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies an external generator and instructions to use it, but those facts do not establish that the creator controls the site or knows its codes are invalid. The description expressly disclaims ownership, while the request for reports about whether codes work leaves room for unsuccessful attempts. A questionable third-party offer is not, by itself, proof that this creator is deceiving viewers.

citations.quote: I am not the owner of this site.
Comment down below if it worked for you

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The disclaimer limits what can be attributed to the creator, but it does not change what he promotes. He directs viewers to the site and says it will generate a promo code, then presents a discount as the result of using one. Asking for feedback does not undo that affirmative pitch. The concern is the promoted route to purported savings, not a proven financial loss or proven ownership of the site.

citations.quote: the website link will be in the description.
It'll generate a promo code for you.
And it'll. Refresh the page and get 10% off your purchase

opening.argument: Judge, the video is framed as a website overview and walks through comparing two discount options on a shopping cart. The speaker even explains that the better option depends on the order amount. That is the language of a practical demonstration: it shows how a shopper would evaluate a code, without establishing that anyone completed a purchase. The narrower reading is a tutorial about trying retail promotions, not a promise of a realized reward.

citations.quote: Website. Overview I do a couple of these not really starting series.

But 10% is actually better on that one
if I was to buy this

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly notes that the speaker demonstrates copying a code, but a demonstration is not evidence of a completed purchase. His own qualification, “if I was to buy this,” limits the claimed outcome. Comparing which discount is better for a given cart is ordinary shopping guidance, even if the source of the codes deserves scrutiny.

citations.quote: if I was to buy this
Refresh this remove the code if you want to see which code is better for you okay.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A purchase need not be completed for the video to promote the offer. The tutorial directs viewers to the external site, tells them a code will be generated, and instructs them to copy it into Lowe's promotion-code field. Calling that sequence an overview does not remove its invitation to obtain purported discounts from the generator; the evidence also does not establish that Lowe's authorized those codes.

citations.quote: the website link will be in the description.
It'll generate a promo code for you.
just go to the promotion code part at Lowe's

opening.argument: Judge, the concrete transaction discussed here is a retail purchase with a promotion code. The speaker describes a 10% option and a $10 discount for an order over $50, then compares which saves more. The sampled cart views show a promotion-code line and changing estimated totals. This record does not show a deposit, an investment return, a recruitment scheme, or a request to surrender credentials. The observed context is discount shopping; the unresolved question of where the codes come from should not be replaced with an assumed, unseen mechanism.

citations.quote: 10% off and $10 off 50 on online orders.
But 10% is actually better on that one

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening calls the generator a suspicious route to savings, but it also acknowledges that the record does not verify invalid codes, failed redemption, or loss. The cart footage shows a promotion-code line and an estimated total; it is at least consistent with the speaker demonstrating a retail discount. Lack of verified authorization warrants caution, but it does not establish a hidden payment or credential-taking scheme.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A scam-like offer need not involve investment, recruitment, or credentials. Here the asserted benefit is easy access to freshly generated retail discounts: the title advertises free generated codes, and the speaker tells viewers to obtain and apply one. Cart totals may illustrate the claim, but they do not independently verify authorization, general code validity, or a completed purchase. The missing mechanisms listed by the defense do not answer the promoted generator mechanism.
